sections.html:
No Arizona county is bigger than Coconino, which stretches across 18,661 square miles with Flagstaff as its hub. Census takers in 2020 found 145,101 residents and 69,108 housing units. Vacancy was high at 25.7%, roughly 41 percent of occupied homes were rentals, and the median age was 32.5 years.

With that profile, plenty of sellers are landlords. Owners of a Flagstaff or Page rental should assemble the tax balance, the tenant file and any repair list ahead of closing. If the house has been a short-term rental, ask the city or county whether its license transfers to a buyer. Tribal reservation land makes up 7,142 square miles here, so have a title company check early on any parcel that touches it. Sedona sits mostly in Yavapai County, so confirm which county bills a Sedona address before you call an office.

The Treasurer's office is at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff and keeps weekday hours from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The Assessor sets the value, and the Treasurer handles bills and payments. Ways to reach or pay the office:

  • Phone: (928) 679-8188 or (877) 500-1818.
  • Email: treasurer@coconino.az.gov.
  • Automated payment line: 877-884-8060. Give your tax account or parcel number.
  • Online: enter an account or parcel number in the Treasurer's portal, pick first half, second half or full payment, and finish on a third-party payment page.

Keep your account or parcel number nearby for any of these methods. Your bill shows it.

A year's tax is split in two. October 1 brings the first half and March 1 the second. Late status begins just after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 for the first half and May 1 for the second, per A.R.S. 42-18052, and a tiny bill of $100 or less is collected whole on October 1.

An open first half is already building interest. The next section covers how to stop that.

Once a bill is delinquent, interest accrues at 16 percent a year, simple, and a part-month counts as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). You can cut it off by paying the whole year before December 31 of the tax year. A delinquency caused by a county mistake carries no interest at all.

An owner who has just paid off a mortgage and then falls behind can ask for a one-time interest waiver, which needs approval from the county board of supervisors.

sections.h2: Timing a listing around the tax calendar
sections.html:
Sellers sometimes list in spring without realizing how the bill calendar shapes the closing. The lien for the year begins January 1. The notice of value lands before March 1 and starts your appeal clock. The second half falls due March 1 and the late date follows in May. The next bill cycle begins October 1 with the first half.

A closing in the middle of those dates means one half may be paid and the other not. Your title company will sort out how the current year's tax is split between you and the buyer, but you can make their job easier by knowing which half is open before you sign. If you are selling a rental, remember that a tenant's rent payments do not change who owes the county.

sections.h2: Papers to keep for your title company
sections.html: Hold on to anything that shows what you have paid: bill stubs, online payment confirmations and any letter from the Treasurer or Assessor. Add your latest notice of value and the parcel number. If you are selling a house you inherited, add proof that you are the person now responsible for the tax, because notices may still be mailed to the previous owner. Handing this folder to escrow at the start saves days of back and forth later.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or a vacant house
sections.html: Many Coconino County houses are not lived in year-round, and rentals turn over often. When a house is empty or tenants have come and gone, bills can pile up at an old mailing address. Update the tax statement address with the county, look through any mail that reached the property, and ask the Treasurer whether more than one year is open. Showing the buyer a clean payoff letter makes the closing smoother than discovering an old balance at the table.

A short phone call answers most of what you need. Ask for the balance owed today, the balance on the date you expect to close, and whether any earlier year is still open. Ask how a payoff is delivered to escrow, and whether the office wants a written request from the title company. Jot down the date of the call and the name of whoever helped you, then pass the figures to your escrow officer.

If anything seems off, such as a payment you made that is not showing, bring your receipt or confirmation. A county mistake is one of the few reasons interest is not collected, and it is much easier to sort out before closing than after.

sections.h2: How the lien works when you sell
sections.html:
Every January 1 the year's tax attaches to the property and ranks ahead of nearly all other liens (A.R.S. 42-17153). Only three events release it: payment in full, a tax sale buyer taking title, or a certificate of removal and abatement.

After a contract is signed, the escrow officer requests the balance from the Treasurer. The amount, plus interest if any, is deducted from what you receive, and payoff lines like this are routine on settlement statements.

Owing tax does not stop a sale from going through. Work through it in this order:

  1. Phone the Treasurer with your parcel number and ask for what is owed.
  2. Learn which pieces are open, whether one half, both, or an older year.
  3. Pass the number to your title company so it is baked into the closing figures.
  4. Sign at escrow. The county gets paid from your proceeds and the lien is cleared.

A cash purchase adds no lender timeline on top of this, so the tax payoff is often the only item on the schedule that depends on a county office.

Fast closings work best when the figures are ready early. A buyer who pays cash and skips an appraisal can sign within days, which only helps if you already know what the Treasurer will want. Ask for the payoff as soon as you have a signed contract, and again a few days before the closing date in case the amount has changed.

The yearly notice of value is your starting point, and state law has the assessor mail it before March 1 (A.R.S. 42-15101). If you disagree with it, you have 60 days from the mailing date to file a petition for review, and a postmark is accepted as the filing date (A.R.S. 42-16051).

In the petition you give your own view of full cash value and explain how you got there. A comparable property works, and so does the recent sale of your house. Separately, when a data error touched a group of properties, the assessor may amend notices within 60 days of mailing. Past that point the roll changes only through an appeal.

Call the Assessor's Office to confirm the dates on your own notice, because the mailing date shifts from year to year.

faqs.q: Where can I pay Coconino County property tax?
faqs.a: Use the Treasurer's online portal, the automated phone line at 877-884-8060, or the counter at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff. Your account or parcel number is the one thing every method asks for.

faqs.q: When is the Treasurer's office open?
faqs.a: Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A quick call to (928) 679-8188 or (877) 500-1818 confirms it before you drive over.

faqs.q: What interest do late Coconino County taxes carry?
faqs.a: Sixteen percent a year, simple. It is not collected if the full year is paid by December 31 or if a county error caused the delinquency.

faqs.q: How long do I have to dispute the assessor's value?
faqs.a: Two months, in practice: the window is sixty days from the mailing date of the notice, and your postmark is your filing date.

faqs.q: Can I close on a Coconino County house with an unpaid tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. Because the bill is a lien, escrow settles it at closing out of your proceeds after getting the balance from the Treasurer.
